# 13-aircaps: sources

Back-test entry `13-aircaps.yaml`. AirCaps, YC Fall 2025 (Launch YC 2025-11-05). Read 2026-10-22.

Sources (short names used below):

- **SITE**: https://www.aircaps.com (testimonials, pricing, how it works)
- **YC-L**: Launch YC post. https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/Olk-aircaps-the-ai-copilot-for-in-person-conversations
- **YC-C**: YC company page. https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/aircaps
- **YALE**: Yale Alumni Magazine. https://yalealumnimagazine.org/articles/6208
- **SD**: Stanford Daily, 2023-02-06 (TranscribeGlass). https://stanforddaily.com/2023/02/06/stanford-startup-transcribeglass-seeks-to-bring-ease-and-affordability-to-assistive-technology/
- **SMI**: Smithsonian Magazine. https://www.smithsonianmag.com/innovation/this-augmented-reality-tool-could-change-communication-for-some-deaf-and-hearing-impaired-people-180982996/
- **T4G**: Tech4Good Awards finalist entry. https://tech4goodawards.com/finalist/transcribeglass/ (quoted through the shortlist; not re-fetched)
- **HT**: HearingTracker, "Hear with Your Eyes: A Review of Live Captioning Glasses". https://www.hearingtracker.com/hearing-glasses/hear-with-your-eyes-five-ar-live-captioning-glasses
- **DTS-ASL**: ASL Deafined blog, "Dinner Table Syndrome: What Deaf, DeafBlind, and Hard of Hearing People Face". https://blog.asldeafined.com/2025/05/dinner-table-syndrome-what-deaf-deafblind-and-hard-of-hearing-people-face/

**Caution:** the origin story comes from the founder's earlier device, TranscribeGlass (about 2017 to 2023), which predates the YC batch. Here it is the founder's own account of where the problem came from, not evidence about AirCaps' buyers.

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (the CONSUMER role, `wearer`; context actor).**
- T4G (through the shortlist): a hard-of-hearing friend who "dropped out of school because day-to-day communication with other students was becoming an insurmountable problem".
- SMI: the friend "found it difficult to understand what teachers and even his friends were saying."
- YALE: the founder began at 16, after a hard-of-hearing classmate in Delhi left school because hearing aids alone did not let him follow his teachers (as read).
- SITE, "Who it's for": "Deaf and Hard of Hearing people" first, then travelers, multilingual families and professionals.

**2. What (the job).**
- YC-L: phones break eye contact and earbuds confuse the audio (as read), so face-to-face conversations get no captions.
- SITE: a private display in the lenses shows the text, visible only to the wearer (as read).
- Job wording ("follow and join a face-to-face conversation") is mine, from these two.

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "When I was sitting around a table, I lost the conversation".
- SD (co-founder with hearing loss): "my understanding drops to 20% at best" in group conversations, where he mostly nods along.
- SMI: "Hearing aids aren't dependable in a lot of situations, especially ones with a lot of background noise."
- *My choice:* occasion "group conversation"; window 7 days; Frequency 4 to 7 days out of 7. That rests on YC-L's power users (6+ hours of daily use, as read) and the ordinary weekly rhythm of meals, work and family.

**4. Which people (segment, market).**
- SITE lists deaf and hard-of-hearing people first. YC-L also names meeting-heavy professionals.
- YALE: a Deaf ASL instructor who does not speak sees the glasses as one-directional.
- *My choice:* the segment is narrowed to "deaf and hard-of-hearing adults in the US who talk with hearing people every week". This is the day-one wedge the origin story points at, and the travellers and professionals came later. Market US: the testimonials and HSA/FSA are US.

**5. Who pays (Buyer and payer).**
- SITE: "HSA/FSA eligible" (as read). One testimonial is from a daughter about her father joining family conversations.
- *My choice:* the wearer decides and pays, and nobody else has to agree (Nobody else, picked).

**6. Mechanism (solution statement, solution_mechanism, compatibility and adoption items).**
- YC-L: captions and notes "displayed on lightweight AR glasses" (as read).
- SITE: four microphones capture nearby speech; the glasses "require a Bluetooth connection to a phone and an internet connection" (as read).
- Compatibility tests "Their phone was with them and online", because the mechanism needs both. Adoption friction tests "Wear the glasses, paired to the phone". Both are my choices from these facts.
- Commitment step "order a pair with free returns": SITE, "15-day risk-free returns".

**7. Price (Price, Existing sacrifice, Ability to pay).**
- SITE: glasses "Starting at $599"; free plan with unlimited captions; "Pro plan: $20/month".
- YALE: "which cost $649 in early 2026". HT's table: "$499 / $699 (Premium $20/mth)".
- *My choice:* the price is put on a year, because the ladder has no one-off: **$599 to $839 a year**. That is the glasses with free captions, up to the glasses plus twelve months of Pro.
- *My choice:* the cost estimate (Existing sacrifice) is **$200 to $1,500 a year**, from the commercial statement's "many already pay for captioning apps and hearing-aid extras". No source gives a figure. SMI notes hearing aids are "often costing thousands of dollars", so the high end stops short of a hearing aid itself. Ability to pay is derived by code: 40% to 420%, some from spend.

**8. Occasions (statements, gate, stories).**
- SITE testimonials: "I could start going to the theatre again"; "With AirCaps I can follow almost all" (at a table with friends); "I can attend speeches and seminars in large spaces and understand words"; a testimonial about an uncaptioned movie theater; one about a father following family conversations.
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups".
- YALE: a first-year deaf in one ear followed three friends in a noisy café. A largely deaf professor found the captions "messing up" at a screening, and they kept him in the loop on a walk drowned by construction noise.

## The respondents

No respondent carries a real person's name; every name is invented. Where a story follows a public account, the occasion is borrowed and the person is not.

- Harriet Coleman: SITE theatre testimonial ("I could start going to the theatre again").
- Walter Nguyen: shortlist reading of SITE ("My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups") and the SITE family-conversation testimonial.
- Diego Herrera: SITE table-with-friends testimonial; DTS-ASL ("if others are facing away or talking too quickly, these visual cues can be lost").
- Amaka Obi: YC-L (phones break eye contact); SMI (phone subtitles leave users "stuck looking at their screens at all times"); SITE work testimonial.
- Ruth Feldman: SITE testimonial on "speeches and seminars in large spaces".
- Tomás Reyes: YALE, the first-year deaf in one ear with three friends in a café.
- Eleanor Park: YALE, the campus walk where construction noise nearly drowned the conversation.
- Colette Marchand: SITE testimonial on an uncaptioned movie theater; YALE screening.
- Andrea Whitlock: YALE, the Deaf ASL instructor who sees the glasses as one-directional and worries institutions could cut services. She is the sceptic who will not adopt.
- Gordon McBride: author's invention, filling a gap: a hearing-aid user whose quiet week went fine, the low-frequency case. It is the other side of SMI's "aren't dependable ... with a lot of background noise".
- Kwame Asante: SD (bars: "I have a really hard time"; "my understanding drops to 20% at best", nodding along).
- Shirin Tehrani: SMI, the late-deafened user who relies "completely on live transcription and captions" and names doctor visits.
- Beatriz Souza: SMI ("Since the app needs the speaker to converse in English, I have not been able to use it much in social settings").
- Hollis Grant: author's invention, filling a gap: a vague, unanchored story so the entry carries one GUESSED reading.
- Naomi Adler: author's invention, filling a gap: a chipped story (rather not say). DTS-ASL on "frustration, anxiety, and even a reluctance to attend social events".
- Frank Dellinger: DTS-ASL (family dinners and gatherings, "talking over each other").
- Ingrid Solberg: author's invention, filling a gap: a counter conversation through a screen and a mask, where lipreading fails. DTS-ASL on lost visual cues.
- Patrick Moran: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No (a quiet week with no hard conversation).
- Lucia Ferraro: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.
- Desmond Hale: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.

## Open

- **The origin story predates the batch.** It is TranscribeGlass's. The day-one founder statements use it as the founders do in the press, but a back-test should weigh it as the founder's lived reason, not as customer evidence.
- **Price conflict.** SITE says $599, YALE $649 (early 2026), and HT $499 / $699. I used SITE's $599, as the price the founder would type today. The year framing ($599 to $839) is mine.
- **The cost estimate is mine.** $200 to $1,500 a year has no public figure behind it. The commercial vector's NOT_HOLDING_UP comes mostly from people who spend nothing today (free phone captions), against that estimate.
- **Two shortlist quotes not re-seen.** My fetch of SITE did not return the "sitting around a table, I lost the conversation" and "My wife appreciates..." quotes verbatim, though it did return the other testimonials. They are cited through the shortlist. The site may rotate testimonials.
- **Relative advantage code.** keel-cloud's `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` accepts only five legacy advantage codes. The benefit is labelled "Following more without asking anyone to repeat" under the nearest code, `less_help_needed`.
- **Checker result.** `instructions/corpus.py` (keel-e2e-eval) loads the file with the registry bound and raises no refusal. `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` reports only "missing top-level 'expected'", which is intentional. Its recount, which is not a golden: PROBLEM PEOPLE_DISAGREE (Frequency: many have it 2 to 3 days a week, not 4 to 7), SOLUTION HOLDING_UP, COMMERCIAL NOT_HOLDING_UP (Existing sacrifice).

screens.why3: I know my own funnel: someone orders a pair, wears it for up to 15 days and keeps it or sends it back.
screens.why4: The only chip is 'Leave this out of the study', which is the right founder-side way out and does not overlap my typed answer.
screens.why5: The belief 'Most deaf or hard-of-hearing adults would order a pair with free returns.' keeps my words exactly, including 'free returns', and adds no 'now', timing or number I did not type.
screens.why7: My step is in base form after 'would', is under 9 words, and keeps 'free returns', the term that defines it. The belief follows the 'Most {actor_plural} would {value}' template without 'now'. The free smaller step that ordering a $599 pair calls for belongs on the next check screen, not this box.
screens.instead: What's the first real step you'd want them to take? If it costs them money, what free step would come before it?

screens.why1: Right after I typed my first real step, checking how strangers will hear it is obviously the next thing to do.
screens.why2: "Order a pair with free returns" is my own wording and plain to me, and the belief and bar read on first pass.
screens.why3: Whether my wearers would order a pair is exactly what I know and care about at launch.
screens.why4: The step is kept, but ordering costs $599 and no free smaller step sits beside it, so a hesitant wearer's soft yes would only be "Probably yes" and not something real to try first.
screens.why5: The step is word for word what I typed, "free returns" kept and nothing added, and the belief says it back faithfully.
screens.why7: Step, belief and bar meet the card, but the step costs the person money and the card then requires a smaller step that costs nothing, which this screen does not carry.
screens.instead: Keep "order a pair with free returns" and add the free smaller step "a video demo of the captions first", so strangers can answer: Yes, I'd order a pair with free returns · Probably, after a video demo of the captions first · Probably not · No.

screens.why1: Right after I named the first step I want people to take, and just before the study goes out, it makes sense to ask whether to collect the people who'd actually try it.
screens.why2: It's a two-word question, and the hint spells out exactly what the respondent will see, so I get it on first read even though 'pilot' is more of a B2B word than a glasses-and-captions one.
screens.why3: Whether I want a list of interested wearers to follow up with is my own call about my own launch.
screens.why4: Yes or no covers it, the two are distinct, and the wording is plain.
screens.why5: My step was 'order a pair with free returns', but the line respondents get only asks them to 'try this for real' and leave an email, so my actual offer doesn't come through.
screens.instead: Offer a pilot? People who say yes see: "Would you order a pair to try, with 15-day free returns? Leave your email." — Yes, ask them / No pilot

screens.why1: Choosing who asks the questions is the natural last setup step before the link goes out, right after the pilot offer.
screens.why2: The hint is plain, but it is long, and it bundles voice, video, typing, credits and text-message delivery into one block I have to read twice.
screens.why3: I can play the two 5-second samples and pick a voice myself, so this is fully within what I know and do.
screens.why4: Daphne and Saskia are distinct and each has a sample, but my respondents are deaf and hard-of-hearing, so the option I'd most want is missing: a captions-first or text-only interviewer, or an ASL signer, rather than just a choice between two spoken voices.
screens.why5: Nothing of AirCaps or my roles leaks into the screen, and it keeps 'deaf or hard-of-hearing adults' exactly as I typed it.
screens.instead: Who should ask deaf or hard-of-hearing adults your questions? Daphne (voice + on-screen text) / Saskia (voice + on-screen text) / Text only, no voice: questions shown as captions, answers typed or tapped.

screens.why1: Right after choosing who asks the questions, it is obvious that I next choose how my respondents answer before the study is sent.
screens.why2: Daphne, read and tap, and let them choose are each described in a line I understand on first reading.
screens.why3: I know my people well: many deaf and hard-of-hearing adults live on captions and text, so I can judge which format suits them.
screens.why4: The three options are distinct, but for deaf respondents the Daphne option leads with asking 'aloud on video', and nothing notes that some of my people, like an ASL signer who does not speak, can only read and type.
screens.why5: It keeps my segment's own words, 'deaf or hard-of-hearing adults', and leaks nothing of AirCaps to the respondent.
screens.instead: How should deaf or hard-of-hearing adults answer? Read and tap (type or tap, no audio needed) / AI interviewer Daphne (every question captioned on screen; answer by typing, tapping or talking) / Let them choose

screens.why1: After choosing how people answer, deciding who receives the link is the obvious last step before sending the study.
screens.why2: The three choices are in plain words I can read once, though 'Contacts page' assumes I know Keel's layout.
screens.why3: I know whether I'm reaching people I know, a searched list, or a group like a Deaf community forum or HLAA chapter, so I can answer from what I actually do.
screens.why4: The three routes are distinct and cover the cases, but for my segment the open group link (posting in a hard-of-hearing community) is a natural fit and its Google sign-in requirement is folded into the option rather than stated as a cost, and there is no mix-and-match choice.
screens.why5: Nothing here touches my product, roles or wording; it is pure logistics and my pick 'People I know by name' is kept.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Not holding up' sits right under the title, and the deciding number is beside it: Existing sacrifice, 1 of 7 lose 12 or more conversations a month, with the bar of 5 of 7 on that card.
screens.why_b2: The tally of 5 beliefs (2 holding, 2 not holding, 1 not reached) over 7 people is plain, but the cards jump from 4 to 6 with no 5, which took me a second look to square with '5 beliefs'.
screens.why_b3: Buyer and payer and Commitment are my exact lines, but Existing sacrifice comes back as about 12 lost conversations a month rather than the $200 to $1,500 a year I estimated, and Price is $599 then $20 a month rather than my $599 to $839 a year, so both are recognisable but reworded.
screens.why_b4: The status lines ('they lose less today than you estimated', 'they value it below your price') tell me what failed but not what to do, such as lowering the price or reworking the cost estimate, and the statement under the title only explains how the interview was built.
screens.why_b5: The n of 7 stays visible and nothing is called strong, but it never says 7 is a small sample, and it shows 6 of 7 'would order a pair' as holding up beside 0 of 7 valuing it at $599 without flagging the clash.
screens.instead: Not holding up on money: 0 of 7 value it at $599 and only 1 of 7 lose 12 or more conversations a month, though 6 of 7 would order with free returns; with only 7 answers, test a lower price or the free-captions plan before trusting that yes.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Not holding up' sits right beside 1 of 7 against a bar of 5 of 7, so I know it failed and by how much.
screens.why_b2: Seven cells over 7 counted is plain, but the marker sits at 5 on an axis that counts conversations from 0 to 15, so it looks like my line is at 5 conversations rather than 12. The unit label 'conversations of the conversations they are in a month' is garbled, and I had to read it twice.
screens.why_b3: I typed a money cost of $200 to $1,500 a year, the money people already spend on captioning apps and hearing-aid extras. This card tests 'about 12 conversations a month', which is a count I never typed, so it is not my belief.
screens.why_b4: The So line says they put it below my estimate and points me to the Price card, but it gives me nothing concrete to do with this result.
screens.why_b5: The n of 7 is visible and flagged as 'a lean, not a call', but 'they lose less today than you estimated' pins a verdict on an estimate I never made.
screens.instead: Ask what they spent in dollars over the last year on captioning apps, hearing-aid extras or CART against my $200 to $1,500 a year, and put the bar marker where my $200 low sits on that axis.

screens.why_b1: The verdict, Not holding up, sits right beside its deciding numbers: 0 of 7 at $599 or more up front, 0 of 7 at $20 or more a month, against a bar of 5 of 7 on each.
screens.why_b2: Each ladder shows its counts per band, my $599 and $20 marked as band low edges, and a strip under each with all 7 against and the marker at 5, so what is counted, over how many, and where the bar sits read at first look.
screens.why_b3: I recognise $599 and $20 a month, but my plan is optional (the free plan has unlimited captions), and the belief drops that word; it reads as if every wearer must pay $20 a month, which is not my price.
screens.why_b4: It names where they landed ($250 to under $599, 6 of 7) but then sends me to the Insights tab; it doesn't say concretely that the up-front price is the problem and the monthly plan is a separate question for my optional Pro tier.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible and the screen says plainly it is a small group, a lean not a call; it claims nothing beyond the seven who answered.
screens.instead: Belief: worth $599 up front, with an optional $20/month Pro plan. So: none of 7 would pay $599 up front, and most put it at $250 to under $599, so the glasses' price is the gap. Few would add Pro at $20, which matters only for the upsell, since captions are free.

screens.why_b1: The status Not reached sits beside its deciding number, 0 of 7 named your price or more, so I know at once that this check never got a chance to run.
screens.why_b2: Three bars at zero and five ghost cells take a second look before I see that five is the floor of people needed and that all seven of my respondents sit outside the chart.
screens.why_b3: My price of $599 up front and $20 a month is there, but money they already spend is a belief Keel derived for me rather than one I checked, and the card does not say so.
screens.why_b4: Waiting until at least 5 name my price is a generic line; the concrete point is that Price failed first, so this card turns on my price, not on where the money comes from.
screens.why_b5: It claims nothing beyond the seven people, says plainly that nobody was asked, and keeps n visible, though Only 0 of 7 reads awkwardly.
screens.instead: Not reached: none of the 7 would pay $599 up front, so nobody was asked where the money would come from; fix Price first, since 6 of 7 named $250 to under $599 and nearly all under $20 a month.

screens.why_b1: The screen says 'Holding up' and puts '6 of 7 decided alone · bar 5 of 7' right under it, so I see that my belief held and the number that decides it.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts who had to agree on their last purchase, the strip shows 7 cells with 6 for and 1 against, and the marker sits at 5 of 7, all clear on first look.
screens.why_b3: The card is titled Buyer and payer and carries the belief word for word as I checked it: the deaf or hard-of-hearing adult decides, and nobody else must agree first.
screens.why_b4: The So line only restates the count; it doesn't tell me what that means for me, which is that the wearer is the one to sell to and that the real block is the price, since Price and Ability to pay both failed.
screens.why_b5: The count line honestly calls 7 people a lean, not a call, but the So line then says flatly 'They decide alone on purchases like this', which reads as a firm fact about everyone.
screens.instead: So: 6 of 7 decided alone (a lean from 7 people), so the wearer is your buyer and you don't need to win over a spouse or family. Price is what stands in the way, not who decides.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits right beside '6 of 7 said yes · bar 5 of 7', so I know it held and by what number.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts the four answers to the order question over 7 people, and the strip puts my bar marker at 5 of 7 with its 1-in-3 rule spelled out, all plain on first look.
screens.why_b3: The card is named Commitment and the belief line is word for word the one I checked, 'Most deaf or hard-of-hearing adults would order a pair with free returns.', though 'You said order a pair with free returns' as the bar line and the trailing 'if it were offered today' are clutter.
screens.why_b4: 'Book them into it' is a pilot-style template line that doesn't say what to do with six people who would order glasses, such as sending them the order link or taking a pre-order, and it ignores that the Price card on this same stage found 0 of 7 at $599.
screens.why_b5: The count line rightly calls 7 'a lean, not a call', but the So line then acts on it as settled, and it never says the question named no price, so a yes here is not a yes at $599.
screens.instead: Holding up, as a lean on 7: 6 of 7 would order a pair with free returns when no price is named, but 0 of 7 valued it at $599, so send those six a pre-order at your real price and see who still says yes.

screens.why_b1: Not holding up sits beside 0 of 7 at $599 up front and 0 of 7 at $20 a month against a bar of 5 of 7, so the verdict and its deciding number are tied.
screens.why_b3: Price is my dimension and the belief line is my $599 up front, then $20 a month, as I checked it.
screens.why_b4: The groups hint at a demo or loaner pair and better multi-speaker pickup, but the screen never says what this means for the price or the offer.
screens.why_b5: Counts stay small and visible (2, 2, 2 of 6 asked, Amaka named as never seeing it) and nothing is claimed beyond the seven.
screens.why_b6: Try-before-buy under stage lights or on a noisy walk, audience questions in a hall, eleven people at a family lunch and one-sided deafness solved by seating are all things I did not type, and every stated value clusters at $250 to under $599.
screens.instead: Every answer sits under $599, mostly $250 to $599 with under $20 a month; test a loaner or demo pair and a lower entry price, and prove multi-speaker pickup before raising value.

screens.why1: As the first screen it checks that I'm the right person before anything else, and talking with hearing people every week is exactly my situation, so I can see why it's asked.
screens.why2: 'Hearing people' is how we say it in the deaf community, and the question is short and plain enough to answer on first reading.
screens.why3: I know straight away whether I talk with hearing people at work, in shops or with family each week.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it completely for a gate, and the screen rightly has no escape option.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's 'talk with hearing people every week' and gives away nothing about any product or plan.
screens.why6: It is one short question that is easy to catch the first time, though the interviewer should add 'Yes or no.' after it as the screener template says.

screens.why1: Right after asking whether I talk with hearing people every week, it makes sense to show me the idea before asking about it.
screens.why2: Glasses, live captions and eye contact are words I use every day; I'd get it on first hearing.
screens.why3: Losing eye contact because I'm reading lips, or looking down at a phone for captions, is exactly what happens to me in conversations with hearing people.
screens.why4: A card to read, with no options.
screens.why5: It shows the idea on purpose and in plain terms, with no odd company words for people like me.
screens.why6: Said aloud, it repeats 'lightweight glasses' and 'live captions inside the lens' twice in a row, so it drags, and 'when the people nearby are talking, you wear' sounds as if I only put them on mid-conversation.
screens.instead: Imagine AirCaps, an app on lightweight glasses that shows live captions inside the lens. When people near you talk, their words appear in the lens as they speak. The people building it believe it would let you read the words while keeping eye contact.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card, asking how often conversations got away from me last month is an obvious place to start on what I deal with today.
screens.why2: "Go without the thread" isn't how I'd say it; I say I lost the thread or couldn't follow, so I had to read it twice to be sure it meant the talk got away from me.
screens.why3: It happens to me all the time at work and in shops, so I know it's real, but a count for a whole month is a guess.
screens.why4: A number box labelled conversations last month, with None and I can't recall kept apart, covers every answer I could give.
screens.why5: Nothing of the product or anyone's roles leaks, and it still asks about falling behind in a fast or noisy conversation with hearing people.
screens.why6: It's short, but "go without the thread" is hard to catch if you hear it only once, and "A number of conversations last month" sounds like a leftover fragment.
screens.why7: One measure, the box, the chips and the escape all meet the card, so both sides stay open; but the verb rule is bent, because "go without" is a vague stand-in for "lose" instead of naming the thing I actually saw go.
screens.instead: Last month, in about how many conversations with hearing people did you stop being able to follow what was being said? [ box ] conversations last month · None · I can't recall

screens.why1: Asking what captioning glasses would be worth makes sense right after the idea card, but it sits under a 'What you do today' kicker, so the turn from my conversations last month to a price is a little abrupt.
screens.why2: 'Up front' and 'a month' are how I already think about paying for hearing gear and caption apps, and the dollar bands are plain on first read or hearing.
screens.why3: I've priced hearing aids, caption phones and live-caption apps, so I can say from my own spending what glasses like this would be worth to me.
screens.why4: Both ladders are complete and don't overlap, each has a clear 'I wouldn't pay for this' and the 'I can't say' chip sits apart, so my true answer is always there.
screens.why5: Only the shown idea, AirCaps glasses with captions, reaches me, with no founder terms or roles leaking in, and a one-off price followed by a monthly plan reads as the founder's own pricing.
screens.why6: Each step reads four short options and then a two-band follow-up, so I can hold every list after one hearing, though there are two prices back to back.
screens.why7: Both ladders have six rungs on the one measure in the stem's units, with a band edge at the founder's $599 (and presumably at the monthly low), two bands plus 'wouldn't pay' against and three for, and the single 'I can't say' escape.

screens.why1: Right after I gave a price, it makes sense to ask what would push that number up for me.
screens.why2: It plays back my own answer the way I'd say it, about $250 to $600 up front, and then asks one plain thing.
screens.why3: I know what I'd need, like captions that keep up in a noisy restaurant or with several people talking, so I can answer from my own life.
screens.why4: There's only a box to type in, so there are no options to judge.
screens.why5: AirCaps is the name from the idea card I was shown, and nothing else from the founder's plan or their words for people leaks in.
screens.why6: It's two short sentences with one question, and the dollar range says easily aloud.

screens.why1: Right after I've put a price on AirCaps, asking whether anyone else had a say the last time I bought hearing gear makes obvious sense.
screens.why2: Plain words I'd use myself; 'something like this' leans on the idea card, but after the AirCaps screens I'd take it as my hearing aids or a captioning gadget.
screens.why3: I know exactly who had a say when I bought my last hearing aids: me, my audiologist's sign-off, or the insurance.
screens.why4: Four distinct answers from 'me alone' to 'not my call', with 'I can't say' set apart; an insurer or a state program deciding still fits 'someone else's call'.
screens.why5: Nothing of the founder's plan or terms for me comes through; it just asks about my own last purchase.
screens.why6: One short question and four short spoken options I can hold by ear, then the single escape; switching 'I' to 'you' when spoken is natural.
screens.why7: The past-tense payer form with 'anyone else' and 'Someone else had to agree' where nobody else is tested, the four in order from alone to someone else's call, and the one 'I can't say' escape apart; the belief can be backed by 'on my own' and refuted by the other three.

screens.why1: After the price and who else had to agree, asking whether I'd actually order a pair is the obvious last question, though the kicker 'What you do today' doesn't quite fit a would-you question.
screens.why2: Ordering a pair of caption glasses with free returns is plain to me; I'd answer it on first reading.
screens.why3: I buy my own hearing gear and know whether I'd order something like this, so I can answer from my own life.
screens.why4: Firm yes, a soft yes that's mine (I'd want to see a working pair first), probably not and no are distinct and cover my real answers.
screens.why5: AirCaps and the glasses come from the idea card I was shown on purpose, and the step reads as the founder's own: order a pair with free returns.
screens.why6: One short question and four short options I can hold in my head when heard once.
screens.why7: The first yes is the founder's paid step in its own verb, the soft yes names a free smaller step (a look at a working pair), there are two for and two against, and there is no escape.
